name: nyanBOX
firmware_note: A fork of the open-source cifertech/nRFBox project with a large pile of ESP32 Wi-Fi and BLE tools bolted on; current builds are binary-only and the repo publishes just a tarball of legacy source.
price_note: USD 220.00 / AUD 330.03 for the Complete Kit - assembled, cased, with battery. Australian vendor. The shop states fulfilment of '4+ weeks' and adds that in practice it is 'often running closer to a few months given current order volume'. The bill of materials - an ESP32-WROOM-32U, three nRF24L01+ modules, a 0.96in OLED, a NeoPixel and a 2500mAh cell - is roughly 25-35 USD in parts, and the legacy source publishes the exact pin map, so the same firmware binary runs on a self-wired board.
skill_note: Menu-driven on a 128x64 OLED with five buttons; no commands, no config files, no SD card to manage.
build_note: Ships assembled but unflashed - you run the vendor's ESP Web Tools flasher in Chrome once, which takes a few minutes.
summary: A 2.4 GHz-only scanner and spammer: an ESP32-WROOM-32U doing all the Wi-Fi and BLE work, plus three nRF24L01+ radios that do coarse energy sweeps of the band and can emit constant-carrier noise. The long feature list is mostly BLE and Wi-Fi signature matching wrapped in a friendly menu with an XP and levelling system. It has no sub-GHz radio, no NFC, no RFID, no infrared and no storage.
honest_take: Almost every headline detector is a few lines of string comparison on a BLE advertisement, and the published source proves it: the Axon detector keeps only devices whose MAC begins 00:25:df and throws away everything else; the skimmer detector matches the literal names 'HC-03', 'HC-05' and 'HC-06'; the Pineapple detector just looks for ':13:37:' in a BSSID. The three nRF24s cannot demodulate Wi-Fi or BLE at all - they give a one-bit above-or-below -64 dBm reading per 1 MHz channel, so the 'spectrum analyzer' is a coarse activity sweep, and the hidden SigKill jammer is three unmodulated carriers, not broadband jamming. Worst of all the current firmware is closed: the repo now ships binaries plus a tarball of old source, so you cannot audit the newer detectors or maintain the thing yourself if the two-person team walks away.
best_for: Seeing what is advertising around you on BLE without learning a CLI
Cheap classroom demos of BLE advertising, beacon spam and captive portals
Casual hunting for Bluetooth trackers you did not put in your own bag
not_for: Sub-GHz, NFC, RFID, iButton or infrared - none of that hardware is on the board
Any kind of real jamming or broadband denial of service
Reliable surveillance-camera detection, which is a moving target this firmware chases with stale signatures
Capturing handshakes or logging a wardrive - there is no SD card

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual-core Xtensa LX6 @240MHz with 2.4GHz Wi-Fi 4 and Bluetooth Classic/LE. The -U suffix means a u.FL connector for an external antenna instead of the PCB trace antenna. It has no USB peripheral at all, so USB HID is impossible.

radios.note: 2.4GHz 802.11b/g/n only. No 5GHz. Promiscuous capture and raw frame TX give deauth, beacon spam and the evil portal.
BLE 4.2 plus Bluetooth Classic in silicon. Every detector in this device except the drone and Flock tools is a BLE advertisement scan.

Three on separate CE/CSN pins (GPIO 5/17, 16/4, 15/2). 126 x 1MHz channels across 2400-2525MHz, GFSK. Used for exactly two things: reading the one-bit RPD register to sweep band activity, and startConstCarrier() to emit unmodulated tones. They cannot receive or decode Wi-Fi, BLE or Zigbee.

hardware.battery_note: Li-Po. The vendor claims up to a full day of typical use; continuous scanning is much shorter.
hardware.storage: None - no microSD slot. Settings and XP live in ESP32 EEPROM emulation.
hardware.case: Plastic enclosure included; colour varies by availability
notable_physical: External antenna connector on the ESP32 module

wifi_scan_24.note: 802.11 scan with per-AP client listing and a channel congestion bar chart

wifi_scan_5.note: The ESP32-WROOM-32U is a 2.4GHz-only radio. There is no 5GHz path in this hardware.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: esp_wifi_set_promiscuous with channel hopping across channels 1-13

wifi_deauth_24.note: The standard ESP32 approach - override ieee80211_raw_frame_sanity_check, then esp_wifi_80211_tx. Targets a chosen AP or individual clients.

wifi_beacon_spam.note: Random names, a supplied list, or cloned nearby SSIDs

wifi_captive_portal.note: Evil Portal with Google, Facebook, Apple, Microsoft and Xfinity credential-harvest templates, auto-cloning a nearby SSID

wifi_evil_twin.note: Rogue AP plus captive portal only. There is no upstream bridging, so a victim gets no internet - obvious to anyone paying attention.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: The firmware adds a passive Packet Monitor with CSV export over USB serial. There is no SD card and no PCAP output, so this is not a practical handshake-capture workflow.

wifi_wardriving.note: No GPS and no storage to log to

ble_scan.note: General BLE scan plus a BLE Inspector that dumps service UUIDs, manufacturer data, TX power and raw payload

ble_advertise.note: Used by every spoofer and spam mode

ble_spam_apple.note: Sour Apple - Apple proximity-pairing popups. Derived from ECTO-1A/AppleJuice and RapierXbox/ESP32-Sour-Apple.

ble_spam_android.note: Sour Droid - a Google Fast Pair and Samsung EasySetup notification flood

ble_hid.note: No HID keyboard or mouse emulation in the firmware

bt_classic.note: The silicon supports Bluetooth Classic but the firmware only ever uses the BLE GAP scanner. This is what breaks the skimmer detector - see detect_skimmer.

ble_sniff.note: Advertising-channel scanning only. It cannot follow a connection or capture a BLE data channel.

ble_tracker_detect.note: AirTag, Tile (service UUID 0xFEED/0xFEEC), Samsung SmartTag (0xFD5A), plus a Device Scout mode that ranks devices by how persistently they follow you

ble_tracker_spoof.note: The AirTag Spoofer clones and rebroadcasts a detected tag's advertisement, singly or in bulk

findmy_track.note: The vendor describes a FindMy Beeper that triggers the speaker on nearby FindMy accessories. It cannot locate a tag on Apple's network - there is no network access.

nrf24_scan.note: Sweeps 128 x 1MHz channels reading the nRF24 RPD register, which is a single bit meaning 'received power above roughly -64 dBm'. Three radios sweep in parallel to speed it up. It is an energy detector, not a demodulator - it cannot tell you what a signal is.

nrf24_jam.note: The SigKill tool, hidden behind a 'dangerous actions' toggle in Settings. It calls RF24 startConstCarrier() at maximum PA on three channels at a time from short per-protocol lists (BLE advertising 2/26/80, 'Wi-Fi' 1-12, Zigbee 11/15/20/25 and so on). That is three unmodulated tones about 1MHz wide, not wideband jamming. It can plausibly disrupt BLE advertising and discovery; against a 20MHz Wi-Fi channel it is mostly noise floor.

mousejack.note: Not implemented. There is no pseudo-promiscuous nRF24 address-length trick and no keystroke injection code anywhere in the firmware, despite three nRF24 radios being present.

ble_jam.note: The same SigKill constant carrier, pointed at nRF24 channels 2/26/80 - which are BLE advertising channels 37, 38 and 39. It denies discovery and advertising in a small radius; it does not reliably break an established connection.

zigbee.note: SigKill has a 'Zigbee' carrier preset but there is no 802.15.4 radio and no ability to receive or decode Zigbee

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. Fixed-function transceivers with a one-bit power flag.

subghz_rx.note: No sub-GHz radio at all. This is the single biggest difference from a Flipper Zero.

usb_hid_inject.note: The ESP32-WROOM-32U has no USB peripheral - USB-C goes to a CP210x serial bridge

scriptable.note: Fixed menu. No scripting, no plugin system, and the current firmware source is not published.

standalone_untethered.note: Battery powered; everything runs on the OLED

detect_flipper.note: Matches BLE 16-bit service UUIDs 0x3081, 0x3082 and 0x3083 - Flipper black, white and transparent. Real and correct, but it only finds a Flipper with Bluetooth on and stock advertising; custom firmware or BT off makes it invisible.

detect_airtag.note: Matches Apple manufacturer-data patterns 1E FF 4C 00 and 4C 00 12 19 in the advertisement. The 0x12/0x19 pattern is the genuine FindMy offline-finding type, but the first pattern matches any 30-byte Apple manufacturer advertisement, so iPhones and AirPods can show up as AirTags.

detect_skimmer.note: An exact string match on BLE device names 'HC-03', 'HC-05' and 'HC-06'. Two problems: HC-05 and HC-06 are Bluetooth Classic SPP modules while the code uses the BLE GAP scanner, so a genuine HC-05 skimmer does not advertise where this is looking; and a real skimmer builder can rename the module with one AT command. Treat a negative result as meaningless.

detect_pineapple.note: Checks whether bytes 2 and 3 of a BSSID are 13 and 37 - a MAC containing ':13:37:'. That is the Hak5 default only; changing the MAC defeats it, and any unrelated device with that MAC pattern is a false positive.

detect_pwnagotchi.note: Pwnagotchi advertises its identity in beacon frames on the Pwngrid, and matching that is straightforward and correct

detect_drone.note: Genuinely real: it parses ASTM F3411 / Open Drone ID Remote ID broadcasts over both Wi-Fi and BLE, giving drone ID, GPS position, altitude, speed and operator ID. This works because Remote ID is broadcast in the clear by regulation. It finds only Remote-ID-compliant drones - it cannot see a drone that does not broadcast.

detect_meshtastic.note: An exact 128-bit BLE service UUID match. Correct method. It finds a Meshtastic node's BLE interface, not its LoRa traffic - there is no LoRa radio here.

detect_surveillance_cam.note: Two separate things. First, a generic Wi-Fi camera detector matching MAC OUIs and frame heuristics for Ring, Nest, Arlo, Wyze, Hikvision and others - reasonable, and it can be paired with a deauther. Second, the Flock Detector for Flock Safety ALPR cameras, which is the shakiest claim in the device. The published source matches SSID substrings ('flock', 'FS Ext Battery', 'Penguin', 'Pigvision'), a 20-entry MAC OUI list and BLE device names. Per the upstream flock-you research this signature set is largely stale: Flock deactivated the camera management access point around December 2025 and the BLE method stopped working in spring 2026, so current detection depends on wildcard probe-request timing plus 802.11 information-element fingerprinting. It is also North America only, and one OUI in the shipped list, cc:cc:cc, is a locally-administered prefix that will generate false hits.

detect_generic_wifi.note: Wi-Fi scan, channel analyser, and a deauth-frame scanner that shows the attacker's MAC and RSSI

legal.notes: Owning it is legal in most places. Using several of its built-in tools is not. In the United States the FCC treats deliberate jamming as prohibited under 47 U.S.C. 333 and has fined companies for Wi-Fi deauthentication specifically, so the SigKill carrier tool and the deauther are the kind of feature you should assume is illegal to point at anything you do not own. The Evil Portal templates capture other people's passwords. The Drone Spoofer broadcasts falsified Remote ID, which is regulated aircraft identification in the US and EU. Check your local law before transmitting anything.

name: KIISU V4B
firmware_note: A genuine GPL-3.0 fork of Flipper Zero official firmware adapted to this board; a second Apache-2.0 firmware on the STM32G4 auxiliary MCU provides the compatibility shim so unmodified Flipper firmwares also run.
price_note: USD 145 from Rabbit Labs, the official US reseller, tariffs and fees included, currently listed as available on backorder. RainWalker in Estonia sells it direct at roughly EUR 77 before VAT and shipping but has disabled direct shipping to the US over tariffs; that listing is a pre-order with a stated 3-5 week lead time. Case, SMA connector, antenna and microSD card are all extra.
skill_note: The software is Flipper firmware, so it is familiar - but this ships as a bare board with a coin cell, you supply and format the microSD, and adding an external antenna means soldering an SMA connector and moving a 0805 capacitor.
build_note: Arrives assembled and preflashed, but you must supply and load a FAT32 microSD with the firmware resource pack before anything works. A 3D-printed case is a separate purchase or print. The external antenna and the LSM303AGR and BME680 sensors are user-soldered.
summary: A credit-card-sized open-hardware board that reimplements the Flipper Zero's peripheral set - CC1101 sub-GHz, ST25R3916 NFC, 125 kHz RFID, infrared, iButton, Flipper-pin-compatible GPIO - around the same STM32WB55 MCU, with a second STM32G4 handling power and Flipper compatibility. It runs real Flipper firmware including Momentum and Unleashed builds, and the schematics are published under CERN-OHL-S. The vendor calls it a development board rather than a consumer product, and means it.
honest_take: This is the real thing rather than a re-skinned ESP32, and it is the only device in this group that touches sub-GHz, NFC, RFID and infrared at all - but it is not a drop-in Flipper. It lacks Flipper Zero's secret keys, so U2F and some sub-GHz protocols will not work under official firmware; the tiny LIR2032 coin cell gives you a fraction of a Flipper's runtime, and putting an ordinary CR2032 in it is a fire hazard; and the built-in 433 MHz ceramic antenna is much worse than a Flipper's, with better range gated behind soldering an SMA connector yourself. You are trading polish, battery and range for a wallet-sized form factor, open schematics and about a third off the price.
best_for: Someone who wants Flipper capability in a card that lives in a wallet
Learning the hardware, because full schematics and both firmwares are published under open licences
Owners in places where buying a Flipper is awkward but a development board is not
not_for: Anyone expecting Flipper polish, battery life or antenna performance
U2F and the sub-GHz protocols that depend on Flipper's secret keys
Complete beginners - it is a bare board that needs an SD card prepared before first boot
Wi-Fi work, which needs an external ESP32 module on the GPIO header exactly like a Flipper

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Cortex-M4 at up to 80MHz for the application plus a Cortex-M0+ radio core running the BLE stack, 1MB flash, 256KB RAM, integrated RTC. The same family as the Flipper Zero's STM32WB55RG.
hardware.mcu_secondary_note: Cortex-M4 at up to 170MHz. It handles power sequencing, battery status and the compatibility shim that lets unmodified Flipper Zero firmware run on this board, with its own firmware repo and its own DFU and SWD path.

radios.note: The same transceiver family as the Flipper Zero. An internal ceramic 433MHz antenna as shipped; an SMA footprint (J301) exists but requires soldering the connector and moving capacitor C315 to C314 to switch antennas.
13.56MHz reader and emulator with a built-in antenna - the same NFC front end as the Flipper Zero
Bluetooth LE via the integrated M0+ radio core. No Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth Classic.

hardware.battery_note: A LIR2032 rechargeable coin cell, typically 35-45mAh. A CR2032 physically fits but must never be used - charging one over USB risks fire, which the manual warns about explicitly. There is also an unpopulated footprint for an external Li-ion pack. Runtime is a small fraction of a Flipper Zero's 2100mAh.
hardware.storage: microSD slot (FAT32; the firmware resource pack must be loaded before first use)
connectivity: SWD1 and SWD2 debug headers (1x6, 1mm pitch)
hardware.gpio: GPIO pins electrically and physically compatible with the Flipper Zero header, so Flipper GPIO add-ons including the ESP32 Wi-Fi dev board work
sensors: LSM303AGR accelerometer and magnetometer (fitted on some revisions only, otherwise user-solderable)
VL53xx range sensor (user-solderable option on the V4BR)
hardware.case: None supplied - 3D-print files on Printables and MakerWorld, or buy a printed case separately
notable_physical: 5-way pad plus OK, Back and Power
SMA footprint for an external sub-GHz antenna

subghz_rx.note: CC1101, the same chip family as the Flipper. The internal antenna is a ceramic 433MHz part and the vendor states plainly that 'antennas performance may vary'.

subghz_tx.note: CC1101 TX. Range with the internal antenna is well below a Flipper Zero's.

subghz_replay.note: Standard Flipper firmware sub-GHz read, save and emulate

subghz_rolling_code.note: The vendor states the board lacks Flipper Zero's secret keys, so some sub-GHz protocols will not work under official firmware. Community builds such as Unleashed and Kiisu-Momentum cover more, as they do on a Flipper.

subghz_bruteforce.note: Via the same community firmware apps a Flipper uses

subghz_external_antenna.note: Needs an SMA board-edge connector soldered to J301 and the 0805 capacitor C315 moved to C314. RainWalker sells the soldering as a service and the antennas separately.

lf_125khz_read.note: RFID reader and emulator with a built-in antenna

lf_125khz_write.note: Via Flipper firmware, same as a Flipper - and with the same limit that only writable blanks such as T5577 can be written

hf_1356_emulate.note: The ST25R3916 supports card emulation, as on the Flipper

mifare_classic_attacks.note: Inherited from Flipper firmware. Performance depends on the firmware build, not the board.

iso15693.note: The ST25R3916 supports it and Flipper firmware exposes it

ir_learn.note: Flipper firmware IR learn and replay

ir_universal_remote.note: Flipper universal remote databases work from the microSD

ibutton_1wire.note: Dedicated iButton reader and emulator pins

ble_scan.note: STM32WB55 BLE, exposed by Flipper firmware

ble_advertise.note: The same BLE stack the Flipper uses

ble_spam_apple.note: Available in community Flipper firmware builds such as Momentum and Unleashed, not in the vendor's stock build

ble_hid.note: Flipper firmware's Bluetooth Remote and BadBLE apps

usb_hid_inject.note: BadUSB via the STM32WB55's USB device peripheral, running Flipper DuckyScript payloads from the microSD

wifi_scan_24.note: No Wi-Fi radio on board. It needs an ESP32 module on the Flipper-compatible GPIO header, exactly like a Flipper Zero.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Same - it requires an external ESP32 Wi-Fi dev board

i2c.note: On the GPIO header, and used internally for the sensors

jtag_swd.note: The board exposes SWD1 and SWD2 headers for programming itself. Using it as a debugger against other targets depends on Flipper community apps, as on a Flipper.

scriptable.note: The Flipper app ecosystem plus DuckyScript

app_store.note: Flipper community apps largely work, but this board is not in Flipper's official app catalogue and some apps assume Flipper-specific hardware or keys

standalone_untethered.note: It runs on the LIR2032 coin cell, but runtime is short enough that most people will keep it on USB or fit an external Li-ion pack

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR. The CC1101 is a fixed-function narrowband transceiver.

import_restricted: United States (indirect) - RainWalker has disabled direct shipping to the US over tariffs; the official route is the Rabbit Labs reseller
legal.notes: Owning it is legal in most places, and being an open-hardware development board rather than a branded consumer gadget has so far kept it clear of the import trouble the Flipper Zero has run into. That is not a guarantee: what it does is what a Flipper does, so transmitting on sub-GHz without a licence, cloning access credentials you do not own, and BadUSB against machines you do not control are all separate offences in most countries. Rainwalker OU states it is not affiliated with Flipper Zero Devices. Check your local law.

name: BLEShark Nano
firmware_note: Closed source. The public repo is archived and its last firmware release was v0.8 in February 2025, while shipping units run v1.1 and later; updates now come over the air from the vendor's own servers.
price_note: USD 49.99 (list 54.99), in stock in both black and clear, assembled and shipped from Vaughan, Ontario, Canada. The sheet's 40 USD is out of date. CAD 71, EUR 52.95, GBP 46. An older Tindie 'prototype' listing is retired.
skill_note: Three buttons and a tiny OLED menu; there is also a documented Rust CLI and SDK if you want to drive it from a computer.
build_note: Ships assembled in a 3D-printed case with firmware installed; updates are over the air.
summary: A 50-dollar pocket toy built on a Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 module with a 0.66in 64x48 OLED, a 500mAh cell and an infrared transmitter and receiver. It does 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi recon and attacks, BLE advertisement spam, IR remote work, a handful of arcade games, and an ESP-NOW mesh mode that links up to sixteen units into one coordinated rig. No sub-GHz, no NFC, no nRF24, no microSD.
honest_take: It is honestly what it says it is at the price, but two claims need correcting. It has no USB HID and physically cannot: the ESP32-C3's USB block is a fixed-function serial/JTAG controller with no OTG, and InfiShark's own documentation concedes the device 'only ever acts as a device, never as a host'. What it calls Bad-BT is a Bluetooth keyboard that the target has to pair with first, which is a far weaker attack than plugging in a rubber ducky. Second, the firmware is closed and the public GitHub repo is archived with nothing in it - so the archived v0.8 binary from early 2025 is the last thing anyone outside the vendor has been able to look at, while shipping units are years past it. If you are in the EU you are also buying a different product: EU firmware ships with deauthentication removed to satisfy the Radio Equipment Directive, and there are community guides devoted to VPNing around the geo-locked update server.
best_for: A cheap, well-certified first device for learning 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and BLE behaviour
IR remote capture and replay in a pocket-sized package
Multi-unit recon - the Shiver mesh linking up to 16 Nanos is genuinely unusual at this price
not_for: USB rubber-ducky style keystroke injection - it is BLE HID and needs pairing
5 GHz networks, which the vendor states plainly are not supported
Sub-GHz, NFC or RFID - none of that hardware exists
Buyers in the EU who want the deauther, which is removed from EU firmware

hardware.mcu_primary_note: ESP32-C3: single-core RISC-V up to 160MHz, 4MB flash, 400KB SRAM, 2.4GHz Wi-Fi 4 and BLE 5, u.FL external antenna connector. Its USB peripheral is a fixed-function Serial/JTAG controller - there is no USB-OTG, so USB HID is impossible on this silicon.

radios.note: 2.4GHz only, channels 1-14 (13 and 14 restricted in some regions). The vendor documents that 5GHz networks are not supported.
BLE 5, used for advertisement spam, scanning, and the Bad-BT keyboard

hardware.battery_note: Li-ion. Vendor now quotes about 7 hours; earlier vendor material said 10 hours and the Tindie prototype listing said '4+ hours while spamming' - the estimate has been revised downward over time.
hardware.charging: USB-C (charging and serial only - it is not a USB host and does not enumerate as anything but a serial port)
hardware.storage: SPIFFS on the module's 4MB flash. No microSD.
notable_physical: u.FL external antenna connector on the XIAO module

wifi_scan_5.note: ESP32-C3 is a 2.4GHz-only radio; the vendor documentation states 5GHz networks are not supported

wifi_monitor_mode.note: Promiscuous capture used by the handshake and PMKID tools

wifi_deauth_24.note: Present in the standard firmware, but REMOVED from EU firmware. The vendor cites new Radio Equipment Directive rules from 1 August 2025; the OTA server geo-selects which build you receive, and two separate community repos exist purely to work around that.

wifi_handshake_capture.note: WPA 4-way EAPOL capture with per-AP, per-SSID and rotating all-APs sweeps, exported as a PCAP zip. 2.4GHz only.

wifi_pmkid.note: Listed by the vendor and exposed through the SDK

wifi_evil_twin.note: Separate Captive Portal and Evil Portal apps

ble_hid.note: This is the 'Bad-BT' feature - a Bluetooth keyboard emulator that runs DuckyScript. The target must pair with it over Bluetooth first and must support BLE HID, which is a much higher bar than a USB attack. Confusingly the upload button in the vendor's file portal is still labelled 'BadUSB Script'.

usb_hid_inject.note: Impossible on this silicon. The ESP32-C3 has only a fixed-function USB Serial/JTAG controller with no OTG mode, which Espressif documents explicitly, and InfiShark's own docs say the Nano 'only ever acts as a device, never as a host'. The 'Wi-Fi adapter' feature works around this by tunnelling IP over the serial port with SLIP, Linux and root only.

usb_payload_lang.note: DuckyScript, delivered over Bluetooth rather than USB

ir_tx.note: TSAL6200 emitter. TV-B-Gone, universal remote and raw transmit apps.

detect_flipper.note: Not in the published feature list

detect_airtag.note: The vendor publishes a separate open-source tool, infishark/airhorn, that triggers AirTag sounds; on-device tracker detection is not in the main feature list

subghz_rx.note: No sub-GHz radio. Confirmed absent from the feature list, the docs tree, the prototype BOM and the SDK command map.

sd_logging.note: No microSD - captures live in SPIFFS on the module's 4MB flash and are pulled off over USB

scriptable.note: There is a real, GPL-3.0 Rust SDK and CLI (infishark/infishark, actively developed) for driving the device from a computer. The device firmware itself is closed and not scriptable on-device.

standalone_untethered.note: Battery powered with an on-device menu

web_ui.note: A file transfer portal for uploading payloads and pulling captures

import_restricted: European Union - not blocked, but EU units ship firmware with the deauthentication feature removed, which the vendor attributes to Radio Equipment Directive rules effective 1 August 2025
legal.notes: This is one of the very few devices in this class with a proper compliance paper trail: FCC Grant of Equipment Authorization and SDoC, Canadian ICES-003, CE RED/EMC/RoHS, UKCA plus a UK PSTI statement, Australian/NZ RCM, and a published security-support commitment through 30 September 2027. Owning it is legal. Using the deauther against networks you do not own is a separate offence in most countries, which is precisely why the EU build ships without it. Channels 13 and 14 are restricted in some regions.

name: Monstatek M1
firmware_note: GPL-3.0 and genuinely original - an STM32CubeIDE project on STM32H5 HAL, FreeRTOS and u8g2, not a port of Flipper Zero firmware and not related to any ESP32 project.
price_note: There is no official store and no official price - monstatek.com has no cart or buy button, and fulfilment runs through a pledge manager for the Kickstarter, which raised 1,364,457 USD from 11,189 backers. The sheet's 165 USD could not be sourced to anything. Observed secondary-market prices are 180-225 USD on eBay for units in hand. Only the M1 Range Enhancer accessory has a retail listing, at 50.99 USD. Delivery has been very slow: at least one backer reports pledging in February 2024 and receiving a unit in February 2026.
skill_note: Feature set and menus are Flipper-like and approachable, but this is an early-production device with reported per-unit hardware faults and no retail support channel.
build_note: Ships assembled. Firmware is built with STM32CubeIDE or CMake and flashed over USB DFU or ST-Link.
summary: A Flipper-shaped multitool built on an STM32H573 - a Cortex-M33 with TrustZone, hardware crypto and PSA Certified Level 3 security, which is a genuinely serious MCU for this class - carrying an Si4463 sub-GHz transceiver, an ST25R3916 NFC front end, a 125 kHz RFID coil, infrared with a bundled database, microSD and USB. It has no radio of its own for Wi-Fi or Bluetooth; an ESP32-C6 co-processor on an SPI link provides those. The firmware is GPL-3.0 and written from scratch.
honest_take: The Si4463 is the one place where this genuinely beats a Flipper Zero: it tunes continuously rather than in three bands and puts out around +20 dBm against the CC1101's +12, though the M1's own firmware only claims 315-915 MHz, which is roughly Flipper territory anyway. Everything else is a warning. The vendor's website is stale enough to be misleading - it advertises Bluetooth 4.2 BR/EDR when the shipping co-processor is an ESP32-C6 that has no Bluetooth Classic at all, and it says 'microSDHC up to 256GB' when microSDHC by definition stops at 32 GB. The GPIO is 5V-capable on the Kickstarter and 3.3V CMOS on the website. There is no shop, no price and no support channel, delivery has run two years behind for some backers, and firmware development has been quiet since June 2026 while the community picks up the slack with an app SDK and desktop companion. The hardware is real and the firmware is honestly open; the operation around it is not a retail business yet.

name: Kode Dot
firmware_note: The product firmware is not published anywhere - the vendor's GitHub org holds only example sketches and small driver shims, and not one of its repositories carries a licence file.
price_note: 199 USD on the vendor storefront, not the 169 in the sheet - that was a campaign-era 'planned retail' figure. Sold against a January 2027 production batch; an April 2027 batch is not open. Kickstarter closed in December 2025 having raised 1,751,547 USD from 8,646 backers, and no independent confirmation of a delivered unit could be found. Accessories are extra: the sub-GHz 'F*CK Module' is 59 USD, Mesh module 59, camera 29, silicone case 12, 32GB microSD 15.
skill_note: The workflow is Arduino IDE, PlatformIO or ESP-IDF - write code, compile, upload. There is no ready-made menu of attacks the way a Flipper or a Marauder build gives you.
build_note: Ships assembled. Apps are installed by taking the microSD to a computer and copying files into category folders; the advertised wireless app marketplace does not exist yet.
summary: A pocket handheld built around an ESP32-P4 application processor with an ESP32-C5 radio co-processor, a 2.13in 502x410 AMOLED with capacitive touch, a 9-axis IMU, NFC, 125 kHz RFID, infrared, haptics, audio and a 20-pin expansion header. The vendor markets it to makers and pentesters, but the security-relevant radio hardware - sub-GHz in particular - lives entirely in optional plug-on modules. In practice it is a very well-specified ESP32 developer handheld rather than a pentest tool.
honest_take: Two things a buyer needs to know before the spec sheet seduces them. First, the device that was crowdfunded is not the device being sold: the campaign design was an ESP32-S3 and the shipping design is an ESP32-P4 plus ESP32-C5, with a different fuel gauge and a different IMU - and the vendor's own documentation site still describes the S3. Second, it is not a security tool out of the box. There is no sub-GHz radio on the mainboard at all; that is the 59-dollar F*CK module, which is gated behind the same January 2027 batch. Add that every repository in the vendor's GitHub org has no licence file at all despite 'open source' branding, that the actual OS is unpublished, that the product page claims 16,000 backers against a public record of 8,646, and that the gen-2 spec grid lists battery capacity as 'TBD' on a 199-dollar product, and the picture is a genuinely impressive bill of materials wrapped in claims that do not survive checking.

firmware_note: The vendor's own GPL-3.0 firmware, written from scratch on ESP-IDF with FreeRTOS and LVGL rather than forked from Marauder or Bruce; the repo labels it beta and incomplete, and ships a Linux simulator so you can try the UI before buying.

Kickstarter closed successfully on 1 January 2026 with 606,237 USD from 4,551 backers against a 7,000 USD goal, and the campaign has since moved to Indiegogo, where the live price could not be read because the page sits behind a Cloudflare challenge. NOT SHIPPING: the last campaign status update, dated May 2026, says 'finishing up our first factory prototypes' and 'preparing for official hardware tests and the beta version of the device' - over three months stale as of today, with no evidence any unit has reached a backer.
skill_note: The on-device UI is menu-driven and approachable, but this is beta firmware on a dual-MCU board where at least one headline feature is documented as not actually driving its radio yet.
build_note: Intended to ship assembled with a case, screws not glue, and 3D-print files published. Firmware updates go over microSD, USB or Wi-Fi, and the C5 co-processor is flashed by the main MCU through a built-in flasher component.
summary: A Brazilian open-source handheld built on an unusual split: an ESP32-P4 application processor, which has no radio at all, driving a 2in colour LCD and USB, paired over SPI with an ESP32-C5 that provides dual-band 2.4 and 5 GHz Wi-Fi 6 and BLE. On top of that sit a CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver with a real .sub file stack, an SX1262 LoRa radio, an ST25R3916 NFC front end, 125 kHz RFID, infrared, microSD, haptics, a speaker and microphone, and a Game Boy emulator. The firmware and per-component documentation are published; the schematics are one revision behind.
honest_take: Of everything in this group this is the most serious piece of engineering - forty-odd documented components, a Linux UI simulator, CI, and a genuine dual-band Wi-Fi implementation whose sniffer really does hop 5 GHz channels 36 to 48 and 149 to 165 rather than just 2.4. It is also the most honest about its own faults, which is how you learn that NFC does not work: the vendor's own documentation says the ST25R3916 shares an SPI bus whose MISO line is tied to LCD reset by a board jumper and cannot be read reliably, so every NFC screen runs a simulation model rather than the radio - while the marketing comparison table on the same company's website ticks NFC as native read, write and emulate. Similarly the site claims 125 kHz read/write/emulate when the shipping driver is a read-only serial reader module. Add that the firmware calls itself beta, that the only published schematics are for an older ESP32-S3 prototype the vendor labels an MVP, and that after 600,000 dollars raised nothing appears to have shipped, and this is a promising project rather than a product.

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual-core RISC-V up to 400MHz with USB 2.0 OTG high-speed and up to 32MB PSRAM. It has no Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth of its own - every radio function is proxied over an SPI bridge to the C5. The USB-OTG is what makes real USB HID BadUSB possible here.
hardware.mcu_secondary_note: Single-core RISC-V @240MHz acting purely as the radio co-processor: dual-band 2.4 and 5GHz Wi-Fi 6 plus BLE 5. Flashed by the P4 through the firmware's own flasher component. Note the sheet's 'ESP32-S3 + ESP32-C5' describes the mid-campaign spec; the S3 was replaced by the P4.

radios.note: Dual band, ~20dBm. The firmware calls esp_wifi_set_band_mode(WIFI_BAND_MODE_AUTO) at init and its promiscuous channel hopper walks 1-13 plus 36/40/44/48 and 149/153/157/161/165, so 5GHz capture is real. DFS channels 52-144 are deliberately skipped.
BLE 5.3 via the Apache NimBLE stack, with scanning, advertising and random address support, ~10dBm

315, 433, 868 and 915MHz ISM bands (driver supports 300-348, 387-464, 779-899 and 900-928MHz) with OOK/ASK and 2-FSK presets, ~10dBm, 26MHz crystal. A PE613050 antenna switch selects the RF path. Driven through the ESP32 RMT peripheral at 1us resolution for pulse-accurate capture and replay.
Semtech LoRa transceiver at 868/915MHz, ~14-20dBm, on the shared SPI bus with its own CS, BUSY and DIO1 lines. Unlocked as a 450,000 USD campaign stretch goal. RESET, TXEN and RXEN are not wired.

13.56MHz front end with a complete driver and protocol stack compiled in - but the shipping UI does not call it. The vendor documents that MISO on the shared SPI3 bus is tied to the LCD reset line by a board jumper and cannot be read reliably, so the NFC screens run a simulation instead. Note the earlier published PCB revision used a PN7150 instead; the NFC chip changed between revisions.

wifi_deauth_5.note: Attempted but unproven. The deauther sets the channel from the scan record's primary channel, so a 5GHz target will be tuned - but stock ESP-IDF's esp_wifi_80211_tx permits only beacon, probe request/response, action and non-QoS data frames on any band. The one community project that specifically studied C5 5GHz deauthentication ships a binary-patched libnet80211.a, because the plain symbol override cannot send management frames with a spoofed source address on the C5's 5GHz radio. TentacleOS ships no such patched blob. Treat any '5GHz deauth' claim as unverified.

legal.notes: Owning it would be legal in most places. The deauther, the captive portal and sub-GHz transmission are the parts that carry risk: deauthenticating networks you do not own and transmitting on licensed sub-GHz bands are separate offences in most countries, and in the United States the FCC has fined businesses specifically for Wi-Fi deauthentication. Kickstarter ran 14 January to 13 February 2026, raising 62,537 USD from 591 backers against a 10,000 USD goal. As of late August 2026 the campaign status is BETA with the first batch shipping and the second batch pending. You cannot buy one: the vendor site has no cart, only an availability waitlist.

summary: A small ESP32-C5 handheld with a 1.3in monochrome OLED, a D-pad and A/B buttons, a Qwiic connector, microSD, an IMU, an IR transmitter and an NFC front end. It splits into four personalities: a maker mode with an I2C scanner and sensor streaming into Home Assistant or Edge Impulse, a motion-to-MIDI performance mode, a genuine wireless security toolkit covering Wi-Fi, BLE, Zigbee and Thread with PCAP export, and an Arduboy-compatible games machine that runs the whole Arduboy library.
honest_take: The security half is more real than the price suggests - the firmware carries a working PicoPass/iCLASS reader with loclass key recovery and Wiegand decoding, MIFARE Classic key discovery, an 802.15.4 sniffer that writes PCAP, Open Drone ID capture and spoofing, and Lua scripting. That is a serious amount of engineering for a 140-dollar gadget. But three things do not line up. The site says MIT licence while the actual repository has no licence file at all, which legally means all rights reserved. The Kickstarter says the default NFC chip is a PN532 with the far more capable ST25R3916 only as a stretch goal, while the firmware's entire NFC stack is written against the ST25R3916 - so which chip is in a shipped unit is genuinely unclear. And the repo's own default build target is the ESP32-C6, which is 2.4 GHz only, even though the whole product is marketed on the C5's 5 GHz. There is also no sub-GHz radio at all, no published battery capacity, and no way to actually order one.

name: Biscuit Pro
firmware_note: Closed source - there is no firmware repository anywhere. The MIT-licensed flasher on GitHub only downloads prebuilt binaries from the vendor's server; current version is v1.5.5, dated 2026-08-31.

summary: A headless, deck-of-cards-sized Wi-Fi and BLE recon box with two radios doing two jobs: an ESP32-C5-WROOM-1 handles all dual-band 2.4 and 5 GHz scanning and attacking, while a separate ESP32-WROOM-32E holds the Bluetooth link to your phone and stores Evil Portal pages. You drive it entirely from a phone app. It genuinely reaches 5 GHz for scanning, raw PCAP capture and EAPOL/PMKID collection - which most devices claiming a C5 do not.
honest_take: The dual-MCU split is real engineering rather than a spec-sheet flourish: because one chip never has to stop scanning to talk to your phone, captures do not drop while you use the app. And the 5 GHz support is documented in the vendor's own wiki rather than only on the sales page, which puts it ahead of most of this category. But three claims do not survive checking. 'Dual-band scanning 2.4 and 5 GHz simultaneously' is not possible - the C5 has one radio, and the vendor's own wiki describes it hopping channels one second at a time. 'BLE 5.0 + Classic' is wrong for the ESP32-WROOM-32E, which Espressif's datasheet puts at Bluetooth 4.2.
